newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan trims taxes in economic reforms package.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan trims taxes in economic reforms package.

text.p: New Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government reduced several taxes on Friday in an economic reforms package that it said would form the basis of talks for an International Monetary Fund (IMF) loan.

Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz said in a speech to the National Assembly (lower house) that any potential loss from the cut in taxes and duties, such as general sales tax, personal income tax and import tariffs, would be offset by increasing the tax base and efficient recoveries.
The assembly still must approve the package, which cuts the maximum import tariff to 45 percent from the existing 65 percent, except for automobiles.
It also would reduce the general sales tax (GST) to 12.5 percent from 18 percent, and personal income tax rates to five to 20 percent from 10 to 35 percent.

Aziz also proposed the introduction of a three percent general sales tax (GST) at the retail level from July 1, initially in large cities, after discussing its details with traders, but said food and medicines would be exempted.

The reforms were proposed less than six weeks after Sharif won a landslide election victory and three months before the end of fiscal 1996/97 (July/June), for which former prime minister Benazir Bhutto introduced a tax-packed budget last June.
Sharif is due to unveil an agricultural package on April 3.

Bhutto was sacked in November by President Farooq Leghari on disputed charges of corruption and misrule. But most analysts blamed high taxes, which led to high prices for commodities, for her party's crushing defeat in the February 3 election.

Aziz said the package would form the basis for proposed talks "in the next few weeks" for an Extended Structural Adjustment Facility loan from the IMF, which suspended a standby loan last week after Pakistan failed to meet conditions.
He said the government also aimed to double exports in dollar value in the next three years by strengthening the manufacturing sector and giving incentives to exports.

A central pillar of the economic recovery programme was a strategy of growth led by exports, which amounted to $8.3 billion in fiscal 1995/96, he said. The duty on machinery import would be cut to 10 percent and raw materials for export would be zero-rated.
"By bringing down the general level of tariffs, we hope to improve the relative profitability of investments in export-oriented sectors," Aziz said.
"Reduction of tariffs on industrial raw materials will stimulate industrial production."

"Any potential loss of revenues is being compensated for by measures like the introduction of a minimum tariff of 10 percent on imports and by recovering the revenues currently foregone due to the concessionary (orders).
"The overall impact of lower taxes as proposed by the finance minister will be positive on the industry," Karachi Stock Exchange president Arif Habib said.
He said the cuts in corporate taxes, general sales tax and income taxes would boost company profits.
